item.title: A New Play in Budapest Signals a Cultural Reawakening for Hungary
item.description:
When she returned in 1989 to the homeland that her family fled after Soviet troops crushed an uprising in 1956, Kati Marton was “filled with great hope” as she watched a “young, skinny bearded guy” shout for Soviet withdrawal.

Then, after she started making annual trips to Budapest, the Hungarian capital and place of her birth, Ms. Marton, a Hungarian-American writer, watched aghast as Viktor Orban, no longer young or skinny but Hungary’s strongman leader, cozied up to the Kremlin and championed what he called “illiberal democracy.”

Media outlets he controlled began denouncing her as a subversive who was plotting to overthrow his government in cahoots with George Soros, the Hungarian-born financier and liberal philanthropist. So she halted her visits home.

After Mr. Orban’s crushing defeat in an April election, Ms. Marton recently returned for her first trip back in eight years to attend the Hungarian premiere of a one-woman play based on her 2009 family memoir, “Enemies of the People.”

The play, also called “Enemies of the People,” about the perils of authoritarianism, might have been staged not at all, or with some risk, were Mr. Orban still in power. Its opening, now that his once seemingly invincible Fidesz party has lost heavily, is being celebrated by the former government’s opponents as a sign of changing times.

It features Erika Marozsan, a prominent Hungarian film and stage actress, playing Ms. Marton as she recounts the ordeals, hidden histories (including their Jewish roots) and infidelities of her parents in postwar Budapest, accompanied by a violinist and accordion player.

Both parents worked as journalists reporting on Stalinist show trials for American wire services, the AP and UPI. They played bridge with American diplomats and cruised around town in a white Studebaker convertible, and they were arrested in 1955, branded enemies of the state and convicted of espionage.

Released amid a brief retreat from hard-line Stalinism, they fled with their two young daughters, Kati and her older sister, Julia, to the United States in 1957 after Soviet troops stomped out an anti-Communist uprising.

Hungary’s recent election, Ms. Marton said, “wasn’t an uprising” but was still “splendid proof that Hungarians were unbowed and that you can only push them so far. They said: ‘No, enough, we don’t want this anymore.’”

The English-language play about her family was performed at the Central European University, a bastion of liberal thinking in Budapest that, like Ms. Marton and much of Hungary’s intelligentsia, is now rejoicing at Mr. Orban’s departure.

Founded in 1991 by Mr. Soros to “promote the values of open society — including free expression and diversity of beliefs,” the university was stripped of its right to issue degrees by a law passed under Mr. Orban in 2017 and relocated most of its teaching to Vienna.

Mathias Moschel, the university’s vice rector, said there were no immediate plans to move students back to Budapest but added that a partial return may be possible now that Mr. Orban, who was prime minister for 20 years in all, had been sidelined.

“All of a sudden, there is a different reality in Hungary, and it is wonderful,” Mr. Moschel said in an interview. Mr. Orban’s ouster, he added, “removed a sword of Damocles hanging over all our heads. You never knew when or if it would fall.”

Not everyone, of course, is celebrating. Hardcore fans of Mr. Orban are in a deep funk as the people they reviled before the election as “woke globalists” and traitorous “Soros agents” return to the fore.

Mr. Orban, passive and mostly silent after his defeat, announced over the weekend that the time had come “to take off the gloves and fight.”

For the moment, however, the “new reality” seems secure, and Hungarians glad to see the back of Mr. Orban are exultant.

“People are smiling again,” said Krisztina Bezi, a schoolteacher who attended the recent premiere in the university auditorium. The play, she said, “would not have happened under Orban.”

Flora Laszlo, the head of the Central European University’s culture unit, said the play could perhaps have been performed before the election but only after careful review of the possible consequences. “We always had to pay attention to the events we organized and the government’s attitude,” she said.

Ms. Marton, addressing the packed auditorium after the show, feted what she called her “second homecoming,” rejoicing that Hungary is now “on the right side of history.”

She had stayed away from her homeland, she explained in an interview, not because she thought she would be arrested but because she wanted to avoid any “risk of harassment, provocation or other unpleasantness” of the kind that often befell people Mr. Orban viewed as enemies.

Among the first acts of the new government was the abolition in June of the Sovereignty Protection Office, a state agency set up in 2023 to investigate people and organizations deemed to be serving foreign interests. The agency had turned its sights on Ms. Marton and several of her associates after an elaborate dirty tricks operation in 2024 targeting Hungarians with ties to a New York-based group, Action for Democracy.

“Like most autocrats or would-be autocrats, Orban needed demons, a constant supply of them, and toward the end I became one,” Ms. Marton said.

For Mr. Orban’s foes, the show’s opening signaled the end of Hungary’s long detour from the European path that was first staked out with the collapse of Communism in 1989.

Attila Punyi, an economist in the audience, said it “feels great to be back in Europe” after years of increasingly close ties between Budapest and Moscow. “I can’t describe how happy we are.”

Ms. Marozsan, the actress, said the play had been conceived before the April election as “an act of rebellion” against Mr. Orban’s seemingly immovable system and as a warning of where he might take Hungary next.

She said she “cried for a day with joy” after Mr. Orban had lost. But she cautioned that Hungary’s new prime minister, Peter Magyar, a onetime Orban ally who is himself a conservative, was unlikely to swiftly satisfy the hopes of Mr. Orban’s many critics in Budapest. “Everything is not going to change overnight so we have to wait and be patient again,” she said.

The mayor of Budapest, Gergely Karacsony, a longstanding liberal standard-bearer, attended the show and said he liked its message. But he lamented that Mr. Magyar had so far done nothing to relieve his city’s financial troubles, which, he said, where exacerbated by the previous government’s hostility toward Hungary’s liberal capital.

Janos Mohacsi, a veteran Hungarian director who wrote the script for the play with his brother, Istvan, said Orban loyalists responsible for his dismissal from teaching and theater jobs still dominated major cultural institutions, including the national theater. “I’m not a vengeful person,” he said, “but they should leave.”

Hungary under Mr. Orban, Mr. Mohacsi said, “was not a police state” but a “mafia state” and it will take years to uproot entrenched networks in the arts, the media, the judiciary and other arms of officialdom. But, he added, “every parallel between this play about the 1950s and our contemporary reality ended with the election.”

item.title: Trump Courts North Korea’s Leader, but Might Need China to Reignite the Flame
item.description:
The overtures from President Trump to one of his favorite dictators came hot and heavy over the summer.

In June, Mr. Trump posted a photo of himself strolling through the tropical grounds of a luxury hotel with Kim Jong-un, the leader of North Korea, during their historic summit in Singapore eight years ago.

Weeks later, he wrote online that the two had a “very good relationship.”

In that post, Mr. Trump announced that the American military would dial back exercises with South Korea, shocking the close U.S. ally and handing Mr. Kim a gift. Three days later, when a reporter asked whether he would meet with Mr. Kim this year, the American president said, “Yeah, I will be.”

The courtship is on. The question in the coming weeks is whether it will be requited.

Mr. Trump is expected to discuss North Korea with Xi Jinping, the leader of China, when Mr. Xi makes a state visit to Washington next week. China is North Korea’s oldest and most important ally.

Mr. Trump said he had spoken with Mr. Xi about North Korea during his visit to Beijing in May, weeks before he posted the photo taken in Singapore.

Mr. Xi is reluctant to have the United States and North Korea grow closer. But he could see helping broker a Trump-Kim summit as a favor to Mr. Trump and a way to gain leverage on other U.S.-China issues, a former Trump administration official said. It would also give Mr. Xi some control over the diplomacy.

For Mr. Trump, a summit with Mr. Kim would help him turn the spotlight away from the unpopular and costly war that he and Israel started against Iran and toward a leader-to-leader relationship that Mr. Trump has treasured since his first term, according to current and former officials and analysts.

Although Mr. Trump and Mr. Kim failed to reach a nuclear agreement during their second summit, in Hanoi, Vietnam, in 2019, the American president still feels a personal bond with the North Korean dictator, they say. He also values spectacle for the sake of spectacle and revels in main character energy.

From Mr. Trump’s perspective, resetting the relationship with North Korea “would be a big win,” said Nicholas J.C. Snyder, a career diplomat who worked in embassies in Asia and in the White House during Mr. Trump’s first administration.

“It’s been on his mind since Day 1,” said Mr. Snyder, now a business consultant and a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, a conservative foreign policy research group. “And it’s also on the mind of those from Trump 1 who came back for Trump 2. It’s part of his administration’s desire to take care of unfinished business in foreign policy.”

A Trump-Kim meeting could be timed to a potential trip by Mr. Trump to an annual Asian economic summit that Mr. Xi will host in southern China in November.

Unlike the Trump-Kim exchanges of effusive letters during the first Trump administration, Mr. Kim has yet to answer the American president’s overtures this time. Mr. Kim’s sister and close aide, Kim Yo-jong, said last month that she knew of no communications between her brother and Mr. Trump.

She also said that any reduction in U.S.-South Korea military exercises would not change “the provocative and offensive nature of them.”

Perhaps Mr. Kim is playing hardball because he thinks he is in a position of strength. He has been testing ballistic missiles and building up a nuclear weapons program while Mr. Trump has been mired in the war with Iran.

Since 2018 during his first term, Mr. Trump has delighted in his diplomacy with Mr. Kim. After an initial summit in Singapore, the two negotiated over North Korea’s nuclear program in Hanoi in February 2019, though they walked away without a deal. The flame seemed to fade. But they stoked the embers four months later, when Mr. Trump became the first American president to step across the border from South Korea into the North, where he shook Mr. Kim’s hand.

Mr. Trump has raved about Mr. Kim — the two “fell in love,” he once said, and he has shown visitors to the White House the “beautiful letters” the two men exchanged. Violating federal records rules, he took the correspondence to his Florida resort, Mar-a-Lago, after he lost the 2020 election.

“I’m not sure there is much more to Trump’s strategy than summitry itself. This is purely about the theatrics of a meeting,” said John Delury, a professor of international politics at the Hopkins-Nanjing Center in China. “I think he’s waiting for Kim to send a positive signal back. Then he’ll tell his team to make it happen.”

“He’s always liked North Korea, even if it didn’t work out well the first time around,” Mr. Delury added.

In past administrations, informal representatives from each country would meet in the hopes of opening the door to official dialogue. But those conversations stopped years ago. During the pandemic, North Korea sealed its borders and halted contact with the outside world.

North Korea has less need to build ties with the United States now. Its economy is stronger than it has been in many years. And the country has bolstered its diplomatic and military positions through its alliances with China and Russia.

Mr. Kim signed a mutual defense agreement with Russia two years after the country’s president, Vladimir V. Putin, ordered a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. North Korean forces have been fighting alongside the Russians against the Ukrainian military. Mr. Kim and Mr. Putin have met in each other’s countries. (A top aide to Mr. Putin said this month that the Russian leader might take part in a group meeting with Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi in China in November, which raises the possibility of a historic four-way summit if Mr. Kim joins.)

North Korea has shown no signs of a softening toward the United States, despite Mr. Trump’s decision to curtail U.S. military exercises with South Korea.

A North Korean Foreign Ministry spokesperson said recent U.S. statements and military actions showed that the United States had “fully reconfirmed its invariable hostile policy to wantonly violate the sovereignty, political system and security interests of the D.P.R.K.,” according to a report in late August by the Korean Central News Agency, an official outlet. (The formal name of North Korea is the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.)

The report also made clear that talks about the denuclearization of North Korea would lead nowhere.

North Korea, the spokesperson said, “can neither be weakened nor be diluted by the U.S. repeated expression of its stand on ‘denuclearization.’” The United States must not “absurdly stick to the past.”

Robert Carlin, a former U.S. intelligence analyst on North Korea, said Mr. Kim had maintained a policy change he enacted in 2021, two years after the Hanoi summit ended in disappointment for the two leaders.

“I think what people have to understand is there has been a tectonic shift in North Korean strategic perceptions and policy,” Mr. Carlin said. “They wouldn’t try to normalize relations with the U.S. And on top of that, there’s an even broader reality. Kim sees the world completely differently now. He sees himself as a leader of the anti-imperialist forces globally.”

Mr. Carlin added that Mr. Kim believes “that a confrontation with the U.S. is inevitable.” Mr. Trump’s war against Iran bolsters that notion, he said.

Decades of American policy on North Korea, including harsh economic sanctions, have failed to deter the advancement of the country’s nuclear weapons program. So leader-to-leader diplomacy is still worth a shot, some analysts say.

“Any morsel of a response at all is good, especially if it leads to a conversation with the United States,” said Jung Pak, a former State Department official and C.I.A. analyst on North Korea.

However, Ms. Pak faulted Mr. Trump for surprising South Korea with his announcement about rolling back military exercises.

“The way it was executed by the Trump administration is not great,” she said. “It made it look as if the alliance is not on an equal footing. The first rule is you make sure your best partner knows about what you’re doing.”

item.title: Eugenia Apostol, Whose Journalism Helped Topple a Dictator, Dies at 100
item.description:
Eugenia Apostol, a Filipino publisher who transformed her women’s magazine into a platform for brave and hard-hitting journalism that helped turn public opinion against the country’s dictator, President Ferdinand Marcos, and who remained a force for independent journalism for decades, died on Sunday in Manila. She was 100.

Her death was confirmed by the Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation, a Manila-based nonprofit that honored Ms. Apostol in 2006 for her work in journalism and press freedoms.

The Ramon Magsaysay Award cited her “important role in recent Philippine political history as an independent-minded and innovative publisher who helped remove from office two disgraced presidents,” referring to Mr. Marcos in 1986 and Joseph Estrada in 2001.

“She is an unlikely crusader in dark times,” the citation continued. “Of a genteel family background, educated in conservative Catholic schools, petite, cheerful and fun-loving, she seems miscast for the role of fearless fighter for political causes.”

Indeed, until 1983, Ms. Apostol’s career was largely devoted to what was known as the “lipstick beat,” printing cooking, beauty and housekeeping tips in her magazine, Mr. & Ms.

A galvanizing moment came that year with the assassination of Mr. Marcos’s chief political rival, Benigno S. Aquino Jr. His funeral procession, numbering more than one million people and lasting well into the night, drew only a brief mention in the Marcos-controlled press.

Ms. Apostol was astounded. “Next day, I said, ‘What’s this?’” she recounted in an oral history called Edsastories in 2011; Edsa refers to a highway in Manila where anti-Marcos protests were centered. “‘Not a single photo of the funeral in the papers, as if nothing happened.’”

“What really got me was The Times Journal,” she said of a leading newspaper controlled by the brother of the first lady, Imelda Marcos. “What they printed was the photo of the spectator who was hit by lightning — that was their top news!”

In response, Ms. Apostol rushed out a tabloid version of Mr. & Ms., which was already pushing the limits of government control for a series on freedom of the press, a highly sensitive topic at the time.

She called the tabloid Mr. & Ms. Special Edition, and it contained 16 pages of photographs showing a vast funeral procession that included images of mourners, Aquino family members and, most shockingly, Mr. Aquino’s body inside its open casket, his face bloodied from his assassination.

The tabloid gained a huge circulation, and she continued to publish it as a weekly supplement. The reporting, mostly by a number of young women journalists, defied censorship and intimidation by the military at a time when almost all publications in the Philippines had bowed to pressure and payoffs.

Her decision came with innumerable risks, challenging the primacy of an anti-communist strongman who decreed martial law from 1972 to 1981, plundered the treasury and was backed for two decades by the United States. “It was very dangerous when she started doing it,” said Alice Villadolid, a journalist who was quoted in the Magsaysay citation. “It was considered very risky to write anything that could upset the Marcoses.”

In February 1985, Ms. Apostol created The Philippine Inquirer, a weekly dedicated to covering the trial of the men accused in the killing of Mr. Aquino. It ceased publication after the acquittal that December of all 26 of the defendants by a three-judge court.

Around that time, Mr. Marcos announced a snap presidential election, and Ms. Apostol responded by starting The Philippine Daily Inquirer to chronicle the roiling People Power Revolution that soon galvanized the country.

Despite Mr. Marcos’s preordained victory, he fled into exile amid a popular revolt, having lost American support. The newspaper, however, continues to operate.

Among her later journalistic enterprises, Ms. Apostol started The Pinoy Times in 1999 and focused the tabloid on amplifying calls for the ouster of President ​Joseph Estrada, a former action-movie star who faced accusations of graft and corruption. The newspaper was written in Taglish, a mixture of Tagalog and English, to reach Mr. Estrada’s base of lower-income supporters.

Ms. Apostol told The International Herald Tribune that while most tabloids “stripped the girls” by publishing racy photographs, The Pinoy Times aimed to “strip the politicians.” She said she wanted her staff to chronicle Mr. Estrada’s “mansions, mistresses and money.”

In her own chauffeured car, she recalled to The Herald Tribune in 2001, she went around the city looking for Mr. Estrada’s properties so she could photograph them surreptitiously. She found 27.

Her newspaper, which sold hundreds of thousands of copies, was said to have contributed to public pressure that led to Mr. Estrada’s impeachment trial in 2000 and resignation the next year.

In 2013, Lakambini Sitoy, a freelance interviewer and blogger, asked Ms. Apostol whether she thought there was “a gap between men and women in terms of journalistic integrity.” She answered categorically: “I think the women are better at it! It’s like caring for a baby, which in journalism is the truth.”

Eugenia Duran, known familiarly as Eggie, was born on Sept. 29, 1925, in Sorsogon City, the capital of the southernmost province of the island of Luzon. She was the second of eight children of Fernando Ballesteros Duran, a doctor and member of the National Assembly, and Vicenta (Obsum) Duran, who oversaw the home.

She attended Holy Ghost College, a secondary school in Manila run mostly by nuns, and showed an early interest in writing and acting in school plays. When her hometown celebrated the end of Japanese occupation and Allied victory in the war, Eggie, fun-loving and vivacious at 19, was named “Miss Liberation” at a local fiesta.

She graduated in 1949 from the University of Santo Tomas with a bachelor’s degree in philosophy and letters. The next year, she married Jose Apostol, an engineer.

Ms. Apostol then moved through a succession of newspaper jobs as editor of women’s sections before starting Mr. & Ms. in the late 1970s.

To edit the special edition, she hired a prominent journalist and friend, Letty Jimenez-Magsanoc, who had been forced to resign from the editorship of Panorama magazine for writing an acerbic editorial that had angered Mr. Marcos.

The two shared an irreverent spirit that gave the publication a compelling energy. In 1983, Ms. Apostol was among a small group of women journalists summoned by the National Intelligence Bureau for interrogation at a military camp, in what the writers said was an attempt to intimidate them.

Asked during her interrogation if Mr. & Ms. had a political agenda, according to Ms. Apostol’s account, she replied that she gives her audience “a balanced menu of entertainment, news, fashion tips, food, medical and family advice.”

“At the same time,” she continued, “we realize that the community is hungry for political items which they may not ordinarily read in other publications, and we try to be of real service on that score.”

She added: “When an injustice is done, we feel we have to call attention to it, but this does not mean we are against the government. We are for peaceful reform; we are opposed to violence in all forms, from all sides.”

Her husband died in 2024. She is survived by a son, Carlos Apostol.

The ouster of Mr. Marcos, and later of Mr. Estrada, failed to bring about the systemic changes Ms. Apostol said she and other Filipinos had hoped for. But The Inquirer did not lose its edginess as it covered repressive leaders like Rodrigo Duterte.

“It’s not just the leadership that must change; the people too must change,” she said in a podcast a few years ago for the Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism. “We did not apply the lessons to daily governance. People themselves haven’t changed. The politicians haven’t changed.”

Ama Sarpomaa contributed reporting.

item.title: Once Home to Batman, This Faded Mansion Is Now Plagued by Real Bats
item.description:
Christian Bale once stalked its grounds as Batman, plotting his caped crusade from its recesses.

But the stately English home that featured in Christopher Nolan’s 2005 film “Batman Begins” has lately hosted another type of bat: the smaller and smellier kind.

Mentmore Towers, the 19th-century Jacobethan estate that served as Wayne Manor and as a backdrop for other movies, was found littered with bat droppings during an inspection by local environmental officials last year. They also found a dead bat.

Spooked by its decline, the authorities in Buckinghamshire, in the countryside northwest of London, are demanding that Mentmore’s owners carry out urgent bat surveys and roof repairs. If not, the officials said, they could move to force the owners to sell the mansion, which holds a Grade I listing, Britain’s highest heritage status.

“Our focus and priority is making sure this Grade I-listed building — well known and well-loved in Buckinghamshire — is protected and preserved,” Peter Strachan, the deputy leader of the local council, said this month.

Conservationists describe the 250-room manor as one of Britain’s finest examples of Jacobethan Revival architecture, an amalgam of Elizabethan and Jacobean styles.

It has been owned by the family trust of the British Syrian property tycoon Simon Halabi since 1998. The local officials gave Mr. Halabi’s family trust a deadline of Oct. 4 to comply with its repair notice and conduct professional bat surveys.

At least two species of bat appeared to be roosting in Mentmore Towers, local inspectors said, based on the droppings found there. The inspectors shared photographs of broken windows, ceiling holes and cracked exterior walls, which they said had offered the bats possible entry routes.

Bats are a protected species in Britain and property owners are legally obligated to take precautions to avoid disturbing them.

In response to the notice, Mr. Halabi’s family said that it had begun a bat survey and a program of repairs and restorations.

“There is an irony in the suggestion that nobody is dealing with the bats when a team of professional ecologists, effectively Mentmore’s own ‘Batman’ team, has already been on the case,” it said in a statement. The Halabi family trust was “absolutely committed to the long-term preservation and restoration of Mentmore Towers,” it added.

The statement argued that Buckinghamshire Council had slowed down the family’s efforts by opposing the construction of a security fence and a storage facility on the grounds. The council said they breached planning rules.

Mentmore Towers is the only major surviving work in Britain by Joseph Paxton, a Victorian innovator best known for designing London’s Crystal Palace, an iron-and-glass symbol of the Industrial Age that burned down in 1936.

Long before it was a filming location — including for Stanley Kubrick’s “Eyes Wide Shut” (1999), the Sacha Baron Cohen comedy “Ali G Indahouse” (2002) and the Spice Girls’ “Goodbye” music video — Mentmore served for over a century as a country palace of the Rothschild banking dynasty.

At one point it was home to a future British prime minister, the Earl of Rosebery, who married into the family. Photographs taken in 1975 show its grand hall dripping in tapestries, with lavish furnishings and a cabinet brimming with trophies.

Hit by British inheritance taxes nearing $7 million in the 1970s, the Rothschild family sold the house and held a flash auction of its furnishings. Over nine days in 1977, nearly 3,000 items of Baroque art, gilded furniture and other treasures were sold, fetching more than $10 million.

The following year, Mentmore was acquired by an organization that promoted transcendental meditation, according to a local history museum. Two decades later, Mr. Halabi’s family trust purchased the property with the idea of converting it into a luxury hotel.

According to court documents filed this month in a separate dispute between Mr. Halabi and a neighbor, the businessman said he ended up keeping the property as a family home after the death in 2003 of his eldest son, who was buried on the estate.

Mr. Halabi has been a fixture in the British news media for years. In the early 2000s, The Times of London named him one of Britain’s wealthiest people, having amassed a portfolio of properties that included a share in the development of the Shard, London’s tallest building. According to public records, he declared bankruptcy in 2010.

Historic England, the government’s heritage adviser, lists Mentmore Towers as a building of “exceptional interest,” a classification that requires owners to protect its architectural significance. The body now says the building is in a “very bad” state and requires urgent repair.

Constructed from 1852 to 1854 in buff sandstone, and noted for its large plate-glass windows, Mentmore took inspiration from Wollaton Hall, an Elizabethan mansion in the city of Nottingham, according to conservationists.

Morgan Ellis Leah, a conservationist at Britain’s Victorian Society, a heritage group, said that the pace of the building’s deterioration was deeply concerning.

“What remains of Mentmore’s interiors are of extraordinary quality: from the Caen stone entrance hall to the 12-meter-high grand hall with its glazed ceiling,” Mr. Leah said.

He commended local officials for trying to safeguard the mansion’s future, but added that the effort “underscores the fragility of the building and the absolute necessity of protecting its setting from further harm.”

item.title: Russia Warns New U.S. Sanctions Law Would Harm Trump’s Peace Efforts
item.description:
Russia has suggested that sweeping new U.S. legislation aimed at pressuring Moscow to end the war in Ukraine will backfire, warning that new U.S. sanctions would risk undoing President Trump’s steps toward peace.

Moscow likely hopes that the president, who signed the bill at the White House on Friday, will rebuff the hawks in Congress and sidestep the law’s harsh provisions.

The law itself makes that easy enough. Its language includes a provision that lets Mr. Trump waive any of the measures against Russia on national security grounds, as long as the White House notifies Congress of its decision.

The law, named after the late Senator Lindsey O. Graham, Republican of South Carolina, gives Mr. Trump the power to target nations importing Russian oil and gas with up to 100 percent tariffs, subject all Russian imports to the United States to up to 500 percent tariffs and take greater aim at Russia’s “shadow fleet” of oil tankers and banking system.

“It constitutes an unfriendly action,” the Kremlin spokesman, Dmitri S. Peskov, said on Thursday of the legislation after it had passed but before it had been signed. “And, of course, the imposition of any additional sanctions by the U.S. definitely will complicate efforts to reach a peaceful resolution in Ukraine.”

He said that the Russian government was monitoring how the legislation progressed.

The Russian Embassy in Washington said in a statement on X that the bill would do a “grand disservice to the current Administration’s efforts to Make America Great Again.”

The Kremlin didn’t immediately comment after the signing of the law, but it angered some of Russia’s hawks. Dmitri A. Medvedev, the former president and the deputy chairman of the Russian Security Council, who is known for bombastic statements that often diverge from the Kremlin’s, called the new law a “Russophobic abomination” in a message Saturday on Telegram. Moscow should respond with “the language of direct military deterrence,” he said.

Whether Mr. Trump will use any of the legislation’s provisions to increase pressure on President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia is an open question. Some critics of the law have suggested that the White House could use the same authority to target the European Union, where a number of countries still import Russian oil and gas. The bloc is aiming to stop all imports next year.

“Given that he has demonstrated very limited desire to put pressure on Putin and Russia, ” Alexander Gabuev, director of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, said of Mr. Trump before the signing on Friday, “my guess is he will sign it and issue waivers and maybe try to use the leverage overall.”

Russian officials may share that expectation.

Grigory Karasin, chairman of the international affairs committee in Russia’s upper chamber of Parliament, said in an interview with the state-controlled news outlet Lenta.ru that various signals from Washington had indicated the United States intended to keep building relations with Russia.

“I’m convinced that these sanctions don’t have much of an impact on the negotiations because we’re talking about serious issues,” Mr. Karasin said.

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine on Friday thanked Mr. Trump for signing the bill, writing on social media that “Senator Graham never doubted for a second that America has enough strength to stand up to dictators and achieve results if it acts THE RIGHT WAY.”

“The best way to honor Lindsey’s memory will be to implement the provisions of this law fully and swiftly,” Mr. Zelensky wrote.

This month, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Mr. Trump’s special envoys, first visited Mr. Putin in Moscow and then met with officials in Ukraine on a diplomatic tour to revive efforts to end the war.

Though Democrats and Republicans in Congress are urging Mr. Trump to step up pressure on the Kremlin, the Trump administration has been considering the opposite. The White House is considering signing business deals with Russia as an inducement to peace before Moscow stops fighting in Ukraine, The New York Times reported this week.

The bill signed into law by Mr. Trump prohibits U.S. investment in Russia, but the White House could provide Congress with a waiver allowing business deals to move forward.

Last year, in his most notable effort to pressure the Kremlin, Mr. Trump imposed sanctions on two top Russian oil firms. He also imposed tariffs on India for buying Russian oil. While the move temporarily caused India to reduce its Russian oil imports, they shot up again after the start of the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran.

Mr. Trump also shied away from penalizing China, the largest buyer of Russian fossil fuels. The government in Beijing has substantial leverage over the United States as a supplier of critical minerals.

Mr. Gabuev, the Carnegie analyst, said China was likely to rebuff any U.S. restrictions, similar to how Beijing responded to Washington’s announcement of an “economic D-Day” against Iran with measures intended to isolate Iran. China has already shown it can withstand Mr. Trump’s pressure during a bruising trade war last year.

“As in the case of Iran, China can stay out of implementation; that is the lifeline for the Russians, though obviously it increases China’s leverage in its relationship with the Russians,” Mr. Gabuev said. He noted that it could mean Russia would have to sell its oil at a greater discount to China.

With oil trading above $100 per barrel because of the war in Iran and food prices fueling inflation in the United States, Mr. Trump may be loath to take any measures against Russia that could worsen the situation at home.

For example, though direct U.S. imports from Russia are minimal, Russia is the second-largest supplier of fertilizer to the United States after Canada. Putting a 500 percent tariff on those imports would most likely harm the United States more in the short term than it would damage Russia, which can sell its fertilizer on the global market.

Daniel Fried, a fellow at the Atlantic Council and a former sanctions coordinator at the State Department, noted that the United States had successfully pressured China and India to reduce purchases of Iranian oil over time during the Obama administration. Mr. Trump could try to do the same with Russian oil, he said, even if it would prove difficult.

Mr. Fried also noted that the Senate passed the bill in August by a veto-proof margin, 86-11.

“Congress doesn’t have to sit by passively hoping that the Oval Office does the right thing,” he said. “They can do something.”

Oleg Matsnev contributed reporting.

item.title: A Small Country’s Huge Windfall From the War in Iran
item.description:
Ferraris and Lamborghinis creep through traffic-choked streets. New steakhouses serve imported cuts of Wagyu beef. Music festivals fly D.J.s in from Miami and Jamaica. Opulent weddings are the talk of the town.

Such luxury trappings are popping up in Georgetown, Guyana’s capital. The city is far removed from the widening war in the Middle East, which has severely restricted energy flows, casting a pall over economies around the world.

But Guyana, a small South American country bordering Venezuela that began producing oil just a few years ago, is reaping a windfall from the turmoil.

The English-speaking nation with just a million people is positioned to take in an estimated $6.5 billion in oil revenue this year, more than double the amount forecast at the start of the year, as the Iran war drives oil prices higher, and countries race to secure supplies far from drone-infested choke points.

This torrent of oil money underscores Guyana’s new standing as a linchpin in a sweeping realignment of global energy markets.

Blunting the loss of Middle Eastern oil, production is surging up and down the Americas, strikingly in Guyana but also in Canada, Brazil, Argentina and, perhaps soon in Venezuela. The Americas now produce around 37 percent of the world’s oil, up from 27 percent a decade ago, according to S&P Global Energy, a research firm.

“Guyana is suddenly punching well above its weight,” said Richard Rambarran, an economist in Georgetown. “But this is only the beginning.” Oil output now stands at about 900,000 barrels a day. Guyana’s production capacity is projected to surge to 1.7 million barrels a day by 2030, Mr. Rambarran noted.

Economic growth reached a staggering 33 percent in the first half of the year, according to government data, making Guyana the world’s fastest-growing economy. But the boom also carries the risk of inciting or magnifying tensions and grievances across the former British colony.

Far from creating a shared prosperity, many in Guyana complain that a small elite is amassing fortunes while ordinary people face rising inflation, rampant corruption, a housing shortage and substandard public services.

The rifts have stark implications for the United States. Guyana is becoming one of the main growth engines for Exxon Mobil, the largest U.S. oil company, as the Trump administration seeks to assert greater control over the Western Hemisphere’s energy resources.

Guyana’s chronically strained ties with neighboring Venezuela are also worsening as Venezuela’s leaders press ahead with a claim to more than half of Guyana’s territory, and Venezuelan migrants pour into Guyana in search of jobs.

Government officials and economists argue that oil revenues are fundamentally improving living standards in what was one of Latin America’s poorest countries, citing tax cuts, new infrastructure like bridges and highways, the elimination of college tuition and one-off cash payments of about $500 to citizens.

Guyana’s population is so small, and its oil so plentiful, that such initiatives are quickly becoming the new normal. The per capita value of Guyana’s oil reserves was recently estimated to be second highest in the world, after Kuwait.

After a state-run ferry capsized in July, killing about 100 people in Guyana’s deadliest event since the 1978 Jonestown mass murder and suicide, some people at vigils and protests asked how this could happen in the world’s fastest-growing economy.

The disaster’s casualties, demonstrators emphasized, were among those still struggling to eke out a living even as Guyana’s government is increasingly flush with oil money.

“We’re sick of hearing about a boom that means nothing to most Guyanese,” said Romola Lucas, a lawyer arrested with other protesters and accused of unlawful assembly after demanding that government officials be held accountable for the tragedy.

As Ms. Lucas emphasized, there can be a jarring disconnect between Guyana’s stunning economic growth and conditions on the ground.

The World Bank has noted Guyana’s rise to high-income status. Annual per capita income in Guyana stands at about $32,000, ahead of every other country in Latin America, including relatively prosperous Uruguay and Chile.

But at street level in the capital, Guyana does not feel like it is suddenly turning into an advanced economy.

Raw sewage flows through Georgetown’s canals. Families cram into squalid housing vulnerable to flooding or fires. Pedestrians take their lives into their hands just to cross anarchic intersections. Robberies at gunpoint are a common hazard.

Georgetown’s rapidly changing cityscape is another point of friction as developers raze the city’s famed, often-decaying Victorian wooden architecture designed for its tropical climate, replacing it with high-rises made of concrete and steel.

“The sheer ugliness of it all is what gets to me,” said Thomas Singh, a professor of economics at the University of Georgetown.

The Iran war’s energy shock has also revealed a paradox: Guyana produces lots of oil but lacks the infrastructure to turn it into fuels like gasoline or diesel. Reliant on imports, Guyana faces high electricity costs and briefly ran short of fuel this spring.

As resentment festers over the uneven gains from the boom, concerns are growing over Guyana’s ability to avoid the all-too-common phenomenon where rapid oil wealth enriches insiders, stokes corruption, unleashes inflation and degrades non-oil sectors of the economy.

Gerry Gouveia Jr., a business leader involved in aviation and lodging ventures, said such fears were overblown. He listed legislation requiring foreign energy companies to utilize local businesses and workers, and Guyana’s creation of a sovereign wealth fund, with limits on what leaders can immediately withdraw, as factors enabling Guyana to avoid those problems.

“Guyana’s leadership knows where other countries got it wrong,” Mr. Gouveia said. Citing infrastructure investments and a robust farming sector, he added, “We’re showing that we have a chance to get this right.”

Guyana’s government did not respond to requests for comment. But in public remarks in recent days, President Irfaan Ali said the economic boom would benefit “every household” in Guyana; he also said authorities were adopting measures to shield citizens from rising inflation.

In the meantime, Guyana’s fractious political system is showing signs of strain.

President Ali, who rose to power in 2020 after one of the most protracted electoral standoffs in modern South American history, has been assailed over whether corruption was involved in his acquisition of a ranch near Georgetown.

He has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing. But by homing in on Mr. Ali’s ranch, Azruddin Mohamed, the opposition leader, seized on public grievances over how some in power, or those aligned with them, are reaping fortunes.

Mr. Mohamed operates under his own cloud of corruption allegations. The Biden administration placed him under sanctions in 2024 in connection to gold smuggling and bribery schemes.

Guyana is also affected by the political and economic turmoil in Venezuela, which lays claim to over half of Guyana’s territory. After Exxon found oil more than a decade ago in the waters off Essequibo, the region in dispute, the feud escalated drastically.

Under its previous leader, Nicolás Maduro, Venezuela intercepted a seismic research vessel hired by Exxon, constructed a military base directly facing the Essequibo border and sprayed a Guyanese military vessel with gunfire.

Less than a year ago, a Venezuelan man was arrested in connection with the detonation of explosives at a Mobil gas station in Georgetown that killed a 6-year-old girl. Authorities called the blast an act of terrorism, raising the possibility that it could be part of a campaign aimed at destabilizing Guyana.

Venezuela’s government rejected any involvement in the attack. When U.S. forces toppled Mr. Maduro in January, many in Guyana thought the dispute would ebb.

But the opposite happened.

Venezuela’s new leader, Delcy Rodríguez, elevated the feud to one of her top foreign policy objectives, even traveling to the International Court of Justice in the Netherlands, part of the United Nations, to present Venezuela’s case.

Her moves have perplexed Guyanese officials, especially after the United States previously showed support for Guyana with defense partnerships and warnings of retaliation if Venezuela attacks Guyana or Exxon.

With the I.C.J.’s ruling in the dispute expected by early 2027, some in Guyana have questioned whether the Trump administration is effectively playing both sides, potentially as a way to exert greater dominance of the energy resources in Essequibo.

“The U.S. does not have friends, only interests,” said Mr. Singh, the economist.

A State Department spokesperson said that President Trump was prioritizing security and prosperity in the Americas, without going into any detail regarding the territorial dispute.

For Guyana, another challenge involves demographics as thousands of migrants, largely from Cuba but also from Venezuela, stream into the country in search of work. Guyana’s government has mostly welcomed this influx as a way to ease labor shortages.

Their arrival is a vivid illustration of the shifting fortunes of Guyana and Venezuela: one country on the rise while the other is trying to exit years of stagnation and decline.

“This place holds opportunity,” said Mirelis Ramos, 39, a Venezuelan migrant who recently arrived in Guyana. She says she even feels at home some days in Bourda Market, a teeming area of open-air stalls where Venezuelan Spanish is heard at every turn. “I see no reason to go back.”

item.title: How Guyana Is Feeding the Profits of the Largest U.S. Oil Company
item.description:
An hour by helicopter from Guyana’s capital, Exxon Mobil’s deepwater production hub in the churning Atlantic Ocean reflects the scale of the company’s wager that Guyana has the makings of a new world oil power.

The helideck comes into focus first, then the mazelike piping and multistory processing equipment that make up the floating, futuristic vessel anchored near the Equator, where more than 160 people work around the clock in 12-hour shifts.

“This could be the closest someone can get to living in an off-world colony,” said Faudia Ramjohn, 28, a Guyanese control room operator who races motorcycles in her spare time.

Exxon’s oil discovery in these waters more than a decade ago ranks among this century’s most significant finds, catapulting Guyana, a former British colony with 1 million inhabitants, into the world’s fastest-growing economy.

The country now produces almost 1 percent of the world’s oil, plugging holes left by geopolitical conflicts. Much of Guyana’s oil flows to Europe, replacing a portion of what the continent used to get from Russia, and some has been making its way to Asia during the Iran war, according to Kpler, a maritime data firm.

As important as Exxon has been for Guyana, the country has also been transformational for the largest U.S. oil company, giving it a lucrative new growth engine at a critical time. Rapidly accelerating production in Guyana helped push Exxon’s overall production to its highest level in more than 40 years last year, contributing an estimated 15 percent of the company’s operating income.

“It’s often said that Exxon saved Guyana,” said Richard Rambarran, a Guyanese economist. “One could also say that Guyana saved Exxon.”

But as Guyana’s oil industry has grown, so have the risks facing Exxon. They include infighting in Guyana’s political system and a territorial feud with neighboring Venezuela preventing Exxon and its partners from exploring in certain areas, as well as the potential for resource nationalism to flare.

Time and again across Latin America, private oil companies have been haunted by political movements seeking to assert greater sovereign control over oil riches.

“Guyana has a terribly bad deal,” said Thomas Singh, an economist at the University of Guyana, referring to the 14.5 percent take that Guyana was getting from the consortium Exxon leads. He and other critics point out that oil-producing countries like Norway or Brazil get a much higher cut.

Alistair Routledge, who leads Exxon’s Guyana operations, said the contract was fair.

“We take all the financial risk,” Mr. Routledge said. “If we don’t find oil and end up developing commercial projects, we never recover that money.”

Attractive as Guyana may now be, Exxon considered dropping the project before striking oil in 2015, worried that investing in a country riddled with failed wells wasn’t worth it, former employees said.

Mr. Routledge also emphasized that while Guyana’s initial take may seem low, the deal includes an escalation mechanism: Exxon’s consortium recently recouped development costs, meaning Guyana’s proceeds will rise, potentially doubling or more from earlier levels.

As for the feud with Venezuela, the United Nations’ top judicial body is expected to rule on the dispute by early next year. However, the decision will address only the land border, according to lawyers representing Guyana. Where that border meets the ocean will determine the beginning of the maritime border, but where it goes from there will be left to the countries to negotiate, they said.

Even as that feud clouds prospects in Guyana, Exxon is considering returning to Venezuela, where it lost control of assets two decades ago in a nationalization.

Mr. Routledge said he expected Venezuela to remain a “very complicated story,” and that returning would hinge on contract terms and conditions allowing Exxon to plan operations as far as 30 years in the future.

Still, citing Venezuela’s colossal oil reserves, which are far more bountiful than Guyana’s, Mr. Routledge added: “We should be there. I mean, this is a large resource. We were an operator there in the past.”

Exxon is also on the hunt for oil and gas in the waters off Trinidad and Tobago, a nearby island nation that has been getting more attention from the world’s biggest oil companies since U.S. forces captured Venezuela’s leader, Nicolás Maduro, in January. Like Guyana, Trinidad shares a maritime border with Venezuela.

In the meantime, expectations have been growing in Guyana for Exxon to do more to raise living standards. Exxon already supports biodiversity research and efforts to boost food production. The company and its partners are also investing $100 million to develop the local work force and improve health care.

Calls for Exxon to expand such initiatives point to a delicate balancing act.

If Exxon refrains from taking on a greater role in assisting Guyana’s government, the company could be seen as neglecting its responsibilities in the country. But if it adopts a more assertive role, Exxon could be accused of infringing on national sovereignty.

“It’s not our job,” Mr. Routledge said regarding the nation-building question. “We’re not elected. We’re not representatives of the people.”

item.title: The Kremlin Has Put Lots of Veterans on the Ballot. Could It Backfire?
item.description:
One candidate participated in Russia’s assault on Mariupol in the first months of the war in Ukraine. Another was part of the brigade accused of killing innocent civilians in the Kyiv suburb of Bucha. A third is a Kremlin-connected war correspondent who was wounded by a Ukrainian drone in 2024.

These are just a few of almost 1,600 candidates officials say are running in parliamentary, regional and local elections across Russia who are veterans of the war in Ukraine.

The elections, being held this weekend, are not going to be nail-biters. The Kremlin has carefully engineered the vote to minimize any real competition.

This year, the governing United Russia party amended its rules to make it easier for veterans, whom President Vladimir V. Putin has called the “new elite,” to get on the slate. It is an illustration of the wider militarization of Russian society, and the first high-profile test of how far the Kremlin is willing to go in empowering veterans in the country’s political life.

“Veterans bring an acute sense of justice” and responsiveness to ordinary citizens’ daily struggles, said Konstantin N. Rizhak, a candidate for the nationalist, socially conservative A Just Russia Party. He fought in Ukraine from October 2022 until July 2023.

He is one of roughly 200 veterans who are competing for spots in the State Duma, Russia’s lower house of Parliament, according to the head of the Central Elections Commission, Elena Pamfilova.

Giving a bigger platform to military elites carries certain risks: The main threat to Mr. Putin’s rule since the start of the war came from an uprising of mercenaries and military hard-liners who said he did not go far enough.

The Kremlin pared down its initial plans to put about 100 veterans in the Duma, which has 450 seats, a sign that the initial zeal for giving such a large platform to a group of former fighters may have been tempered.

Mikhail Komin, an analyst with the Center for European Policy Analysis and author of a recent paper on Russian veterans in politics, said that according to his analysis of the candidate lists put forth by the United Russia party, about 50 candidates are poised to win spots in the Duma.

The party has tried to balance battle-hardened former combatants with those who previously held managerial roles and then saw that a stint in uniform could improve their positions, Mr. Komin said.

“In mixing real combatants with ‘nominal’ combatants,” he said in a phone interview from Washington, the authorities were “deliberately trying to prevent any kind of autonomy from this potential political group in the Parliament consisting of veterans.”

But Mr. Komin said the presence of so many former fighters in the government could “put pressure on bureaucratic and business elites to demonstrate their loyalty to the military by extending tangible support for the war.”

A large, vocal group of veterans could become a powerful bloc to stymie a cease-fire or postwar reconciliation efforts, Mr. Komin argued.

Though Mr. Rizhak, the veteran candidate, is not from the governing party, he represents a group of Kremlin-preferred veterans who have high-level work experience and are not tying their candidacies solely to the war.

After being decommissioned because he has many children — Mr. Rizhak’s wife is currently expecting their eighth child, a seventh son — he returned to work at Russia’s state-owned nuclear energy corporation, Rosatom. He said his work experience was the reason people should vote for him, with his military service just one part of his background.

It is not a foregone conclusion that the wider populace will accept the veterans as the heroes the Kremlin has trumpeted them to be. Many Russians believe soldiers fought for personal gain and feel wary of the creeping militarization of politics. Others say they worry that a hard-line military bloc could pose political problems in the postwar future.

One potential voter, Marat, 31 — who asked that his surname be withheld because of fears for his personal safety — expressed deep hostility and cynicism toward veteran candidates. “Half are from prison, half are brainless,” he said during a smoke break near the liquor store where he works in central Moscow, referring to the military recruitment drives in prisons. He said he would not vote.

Mr. Putin called veterans of the Ukraine war “the true elite of Russia” in February 2024, when he announced the highly selective “Time of Heroes” program, which offers executive education and work placement to former fighters. The newly minted leaders, he said, would become the group to which “Russia might one day be entrusted,” supplanting an elite that “lined their pockets in the 1990s.”

Independent Russian journalists determined that more than a dozen participants in the program had been accused of war crimes.

A number of the candidates running participated in the Time of Heroes program. Among them is Vladislav Golovin, 29, who lost part of his leg in fighting in Mariupol, Ukraine, and now runs the Yunarmia, a Kremlin-conceived military-patriotic youth movement, for which he is under Western sanctions.

Larisa, 66, a retired medic from the Siberian city of Krasnoyarsk — who also asked that her surname be withheld because of her fear of talking to an American media outlet — said she was open to having veterans at all levels of government.

They had “experienced real hardship,” she said, and could contribute positively to society, though she said her primary criterion was “managerial skills.” She said she would be voting for United Russia.

Aleksei A. Venediktov, the former editor in chief of the liberal Echo of Moscow radio station, which was shut down in the early days of the war, downplayed the role the handpicked veterans could have in the Duma.

“Everyone knows,” he said, that members of the Duma “will vote as they are told.”

The presence of veterans in the election is indicative of the wider militarization of Russian society. If, in the early days of the invasion of Ukraine, leaders called it a “Special Military Operation” that would minimally affect people’s lives, rather than a full-scale war, now the state has sought to promote veterans and fallen soldiers everywhere: on television, in movies, in schools — and even in a new metro station in Moscow.

The station, on the Rublyovo-Arkhangelskaya line, features bas-reliefs of soldiers alongside drones and military equipment.

Mr. Rizhak, the veteran candidate, said he was in favor of political pluralism, and even went so far as to say that it was wrong for the Central Elections Commission to remove the antiwar Yabloko party from the ballot, even though he disagreed with their platform of an immediate cease-fire.

“No normal person advocates for war,” he said. “All normal people want peace.”

But Mr. Rizhak said ending the war right now would mean his fallen comrades had died in vain.

“Sometimes,” he said, “the path to peace lies through war.”

item.title: Millionaire Activist Seeks Asylum in Spain
item.description:
James Chambers is a former heir to a media fortune who broke with his family a few years ago in a deal he said was worth “hundreds of millions.” He reveres Stalin and Mao, and calls the United States a “murder-for-profit scheme.”

After the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel ignited the war in Gaza, Mr. Chambers championed the Palestinian militant group. He attended some protests and paid bail and legal fees for people arrested at actions targeting American branches of Elbit Systems, an Israeli defense contractor, including members of the Berkshire Communists, his Massachusetts collective.

Now, Mr. Chambers, 41, is in jail in Spain, fighting an extradition request from the United States. He was arrested in Ibiza in July, and a council of Spanish government ministers is expected to consider the issue on Tuesday.

The extradition request comes amid high tensions between Spain and the United States. President Trump and Pedro Sánchez, the left-wing Spanish prime minister, have clashed over trade, military spending and the war in Iran. Mr. Sánchez has called Israel’s prosecution of the war in Gaza a genocide, and Spain recognizes the state of Palestine, positions the United States has not taken.

Mr. Chambers’s arrest this summer generated international headlines and has become a cause célèbre for some prominent political and cultural figures in Spain and other parts of the world.

The United States has not unsealed the charges against Mr. Chambers, but Baltasar Garzón, his lawyer in Spain, said the government was claiming disorderly conduct and conspiracy to riot related to the 2023 protests, as well as money laundering to ultimately fund terrorism.

Mr. Garzón, a former judge who achieved global fame for his aggressive efforts to extradite human rights abusers to Spain, dismissed the U.S. case as “strictly political,” saying through a translator in an interview that it was part of a wider U.S. campaign against “people who have a concrete stand on Palestine.”

The U.S. money laundering accusation is tied to a transfer of more than $7 million to Tunisia after Mr. Chambers left the United States, funds that paid debts and salaries for a Tunisian soccer team, his lawyer said. Mr. Chambers has also contributed more than $1 million to humanitarian organizations in Gaza that help orphans and other children, as well as provide food and water in the devastated enclave, the lawyer said.

His client’s money comes from the deal he made with his family to cut ties in 2023 with its conglomerate, Cox Enterprises, and was spent on legal causes, Mr. Garzón said.

The defense contends that the United States aims to taint Mr. Chambers’s legitimate donations based on his stated opinions, criminalizing aid to Palestinians. It has submitted a brief to the Spanish government contesting the charges and arguing that the claimed offenses do not meet extradition criteria and risk chilling free speech, among other issues, Mr. Garzón said.

“We suspect, if he were extradited, he would not be granted a fair trial,” he added.

The U.S. Department of Justice declined to comment, and representatives of Spain in Washington did not respond to queries.

Pressure is growing in Spain to limit cooperation with the United States.

Ione Belarra, a member of Spain’s Congress of Deputies and secretary general of the left-wing Podemos party, said that Mr. Chambers, known as Fergie, “is the first political prisoner in Spanish history being imprisoned because of his support for Palestine.”

About 150 prominent artists, activists and academics from around the world on Friday joined a letter calling on Spain to reject the extradition request and protect Mr. Chambers. The actors Richard Gere, Cynthia Nixon, Natasha Lyonne and Viggo Mortensen, the activists Angela Davis and Greta Thunberg, and the philosopher Judith Butler are among them.

Mr. Chambers’s wife, Stella Schnabel, an actor and daughter of the artist and director Julian Schnabel, has also been campaigning for her husband’s release. “Fergie is a devoted philanthropist committed to supporting global humanitarian efforts,” she said in a statement to The New York Times. “I am urging the Spanish government to reject Fergie’s political persecution and send a message that solidarity with Palestinians is not a crime.”

Mr. Garzón argues that, while his client has expressed opinions that are unpopular with the U.S. government and has supported activists and humanitarian causes, he has committed no crimes. Though some members of his collective faced prosecution for an action causing damage at Elbit Systems in New Hampshire in November 2023 and pleaded guilty to criminal mischief and criminal trespassing, Mr. Chambers was not arrested or charged, Mr. Garzón noted.

If the extradition request were rejected, Mr. Chambers would be freed. If it were accepted, there would be additional steps, including going to the judiciary and perhaps back to the government, which could take a year or more, Mr. Garzón said.

But Mr. Chambers has no intention of going home, his lawyer said, and has begun seeking asylum in Spain, arguing that he will face political persecution if extradited.

item.title: Behold the Most Handsome Melons in Mexico
item.description:
The line stretched the entire length of the steep cobblestone bridge in the historic part of town. Many had waited a year to participate in the event and were anxious to register before the spots filled up.

All of them held the same thing in their hands on Tuesday afternoon: a melon.

Mexico is full of unique and vibrant traditions, both ancient and new. There is a century-old radish-carving competition, and a race of people with potbellies in Oaxaca State. There is a mascot obstacle dash in Mexico City.

The annual melon race in Xalapa is not only one of Mexico’s most colorful traditions but also one of its most random. What began as a mockumentary among friends two decades ago — filming melons racing down the city’s sloping cobblestone bridge while streets were closed on Mexican Independence Day — morphed into a yearly tradition, drawing hundreds of participants and thousands of spectators.

“I really love seeing people come together for something that isn’t just mindlessly spending money,” said Sabrina Salem, 28, an actress from Xalapa who lives in Spain but planned a visit back to see her family during the melon race.

“Plus it’s seeing your city united by something that’s absurd,” she added. “To me, that feels like the most Mexican thing ever.”

TEXAS

mexico

VERACRUZ

Xalapa

Mexico City

300 miles

The New York Times

Xalapa, the capital of Veracruz State in eastern Mexico, is often known as a surrealist city. Its nearly half a million people are surrounded by volcanoes and cloud forests, which creates a daily fog that adds a magical element. It is dotted with steep, winding cobblestone streets. House numbers sometimes lack logical order and skip around in odd ways. A local tradition has diners eating pizza with yogurt.

“I wouldn’t say that just Xalapa is surreal, but various places in Mexico,” said Kevin Sameer, 25, wearing a Spiderman lucha libre mask and holding a melon decorated in the same style. “You could keep walking on the bridge here and say, ‘Hey, why is there a gorilla planted on top of that building?’”

(There is indeed a large gorilla statue on top of a nearby building.)

“But there are artistic and novel things that you’d hardly see anywhere else in the world, only here,” he added.

Manuel López Rocha, 39, one of the original organizers of the race, said that he and his friends never ended up finishing the mockumentary because people started cheering and betting on the fastest melons. The following year, he said, his friends decided to hold the race again — and it caught on.

“Because, ultimately, it’s people going out into the street to play,” he said. “That’s really powerful. And it has been especially powerful during times when the city was going through really difficult moments.”

A group of 10 residents, including Mr. López Rocha, a university professor, volunteer to organize the annual event. They find local businesses to sponsor it. The prizes are coupons to those places, such as free cinnamon rolls from a bakery, a haircut from a barbershop and a consultation with a psychotherapist.

A few years into annual race, Mr. López Rocha said they added another competition: the most handsome melon.

Anyone can participate in either contest. They are free and held rain or shine. Participants must use a melon of any size of the Cucumis melo species — honeydew or cantaloupe — for the race. (Sorry, watermelons.) Prizes are awarded for most handsome for the children’s and general categories, and to the top three finishers in the race.

The most handsome melons are determined by applause. People filled a square underneath the bridge to judge, many peering over the sides to hoot and holler for their favorite fruit.

There were melons decorated with serious themes, such as a woman in a wheelchair, submitted by a local group of survivors of sexual violence. A group of researchers entered a melon decorated as a vulture, hoping to raise awareness about the bird’s importance to the ecosystem.

And there were melons decorated with more comical themes or pop culture, from Minions to Charlie Brown to Pokémon.

Ms. Salem and her girlfriend, Anna Marchessi, 34, a Spanish actress and screenwriter also visiting from Madrid, had two entries: a depiction of the famous Olmec colossal head statue at Xalapa’s anthropology museum and another of President Trump, who recently said Mexico offered the United States few things it needed beyond tamales.

Their Trump melon showed him selling tamales with the words, Make Melones Great Again.

“We get pleasure from seeing Trump’s head roll around here,” Ms. Salem said.

The three entries that won in the general category all depicted themes from Mexican culture. First place used six small melons to recreate the ancient Indigenous ceremony of the Veracruz fliers, who spin atop a tall pole. The runners-up portrayed the famous Mexican singer Juan Gabriel, during his well-known Palace of Fine Arts performance, and a traditional Veracruz musician of Son Jarocho, an energetic, communal folk genre, with the melon’s arm moving to play a small guitar-like instrument.

Diego Mortera, 40, and Ángel Mena, 32, said they decorated their Veracruz musician melon in five hours. The friends met in Xalapa last year and decided to compete after hearing so many residents talk about the event.

Others have been competing for many years.

Mara Yerena, 36, an architect from Xalapa, has participated 15 times. She said the entries have gotten more elaborate over the years and she loved how the event fostered a sense of community, with so many young people participating.

She and her friend, Marbet Salazar, 39, also an architect who was visiting from Mexico City just for the race, won second place in the race last year. This year, they finished third.

For the race, there were nine rounds of 25 melons each, with the top five advancing to the two semifinals and then the top 10 from each to the final. The melons were lined up at the top of the cobblestone bridge and then all released at the same time.

Some zipped downhill, while others bounced slowly over the bumpy street. The sidewalks of the bridge were stuffed with spectators, cheering on slow melons and laughing as participants chased after their rolling fruit.

“I didn’t think it would get so crowded,” said Marcel Trinidad, 21.

She and Iván González, 22, medical students at a local university, finished first in the race and walked away with their arms full of gifts, coupons, a plaque, a trophy and their nine-pound melon with a snail painted on it. They bought it for $9 at a market earlier in the day.

The secret to picking a winning melon? “It has to be very round, smooth and have lots of luck,” Ms. Yerena said.

item.title: Rejecting Trump, South Korean Leader Says He Will Not Send Troops to Iran
item.description:
President Lee Jae​ Myung of South Korea pushed back against pressure from the Trump administration on Friday, declaring that his country would not deploy troops or military assets to support the U.S.-led war against Iran.

In recent weeks, President Trump has publicly taunted the South Korean leader, venting frustration over ​what he described as Seoul’s refusal to help defend the Strait of Hormuz — once the world’s main transit point for oil — while American troops remain stationed on​ ​the Korean Peninsula to shield ​South Korea from North Korea.​ On Friday, Mr. Lee ​firmly rejected any ​military involvement in the Middle East conflict.

“There will be no deployment of troops or dispatch of military assets to​ be involved in or intervene in this war,” Mr. Lee said in a news conference.

Instead of a combat deployment, Mr. Lee noted that Seoul is considering expanding the operational scope of a South Korean navy destroyer and its support ships currently stationed off the coast of Somalia for antipiracy operations. He emphasized that even if those assets move closer to the Red Sea or the Strait of Hormuz, their sole focus would be protecting South Korean ​oil tankers and other commercial vessels. They will not participate in any operations that could be interpreted as supporting the war against Iran​, he said.

​While Mr. Trump has not specified the exact type of assistance he expects from Seoul, he complained last month that he had asked Mr. Lee “to give us a little hand” in the conflict, reminding him of the U.S. military presence in South Korea.

“He said, ‘No, thanks,’” Mr. Trump ​recalled. “I see. Well, why are we involved in helping you?”

It was not the only issue that a grim-faced Mr. Lee addressed on Friday. Fifteen months into his single five-year term, his approval rating has fallen to a new low of 37 percent, battered by troubles brewing not only at home but also by strains with South Korea’s most important ally, the United States.

Last month, Mr. Trump unilaterally scaled down one of the United States’ annual joint military exercises with South Korea, calling the drills not only “costly” but also “totally inappropriate and hostile” toward North Korea. He said that, for as long as he had been in office, North Korea had been “unthreatening and respectful.” Mr. Trump also boasted of having a “very good relationship” with North Korea’s leader, Kim Jong-un, even as the North has become a bigger nuclear threat against the South.

At home, South Korea’s main stock index — once lauded as a premier beneficiary of the global A.I. boom — has crashed, devastating the portfolios of millions of individual investors who were encouraged by Mr. Lee’s government to buy stocks. Mr. Lee has also failed to deliver on his repeated pledges to curb rising housing costs.

The opposition has accused him of seeking a constitutional amendment that would allow him to run for a second term, a move explicitly barred by the current Constitution. His presidency also remains marred by his suspended criminal trials on charges including violating election laws and inducing perjury. The opposition has claimed that Mr. Lee was plotting a special bill to erase those charges, ​which he has insisted were fabrications orchestrated by his conservative adversary and predecessor, the impeached and ousted former President Yoon Suk Yeol.

On Friday, Mr. Lee said that although he supported a constitutional revision allowing future presidents to seek a second term, he himself had no intention of seeking re-election. He called it “constitutionally impossible​.” The claim that he might ​seek a second term, he said, was nothing more than a “political offensive.”

Mr. Lee also said he supported the National Assembly’s appointment of a special prosecutor to investigate whether politicians like him, as well as journalists, had been targeted in politically motivated criminal investigations under Mr. Yoon. But he said that he did not want such a special prosecutor to have the power to drop the criminal charges already filed against him.

“It’s because of my own shortcomings,” Mr. Lee said, referring to his plummeting approval ratings. “I fell short in consideration, sensitivity and communication.”

Mr. Lee also said his government remained in “fierce” negotiations with Washington over how to implement the sweeping agreement the two governments announced last November. Under the pact, Mr. Trump reduced tariffs on key South Korean exports, including automobiles, from 25 percent to 15 percent. He also pledged U.S. support for South Korea’s efforts to develop nuclear-powered submarines and to enrich uranium for civilian nuclear energy. In exchange, Mr. Lee committed $350 billion in investments in the United States.

But negotiations over the deal’s implementation have stalled over the details, fueling doubts on both sides about the other’s willingness to follow through.

On Friday, Mr. Lee said the two governments were close to finalizing an agreement on where the first batch of South Korean investments should go.

Mr. Lee said he had been unhappy with a proposed agreement and had instructed his government to continue negotiating. He did not elaborate, but emphasized that any investment projects must be “commercially reasonable” and that the two governments needed to agree on how to share profits and losses from such projects.

“We should not buckle under pressure or coercion,” he said, adding that his comment reflected his government’s general negotiating principle and was not aimed at the Trump administration in particular.

But Mr. Trump’s complaints that he has received “very little help from other countries” for the war in Iran have placed immense diplomatic pressure on Seoul. The United States led the United Nations forces that repelled North Korean invaders during the 1950-53 Korean War, anchoring what is now a seven-decade-long alliance. South Korean troops formed the largest foreign contingent fighting alongside American forces in the Vietnam War.

Yet, acceding to Mr. Trump’s request would carry severe political risks for Mr. Lee. The last time South Korea sent forces to a U.S.-led conflict — the Iraq War, which began in 2003 — the progressive administration of then-President Roh Moo-hyun faced a fierce domestic backlash, particularly from his own party and base. Although that deployment consisted primarily of engineering and medical units, the decision permanently crippled Mr. Roh’s approval ratings.

Public opinion in South Korea remains against intervention. A poll conducted this month showed that 55 percent of South Koreans oppose deploying troops to the conflict with Iran, compared to just 32 percent in favor.

item.title: Plucked From Obscurity, a French Outpost Navigates the Spotlight
item.description:
The last outpost of France’s once-vast colonial empire in North America, the tiny archipelago of Saint Pierre and Miquelon is nearly encircled by Canada and far closer to the United States than to Paris. Marooned, perhaps, but safe in the anonymity of the world’s lost corners.

Then, three recent events yanked it from obscurity: a hit television series from Canada, a political insult from France and tariffs — of course — from the United States.

“All of a sudden, these three developments have made us very much in demand,” said Yannick Abraham, a vice president of the territory’s government, in his office in Saint Pierre, a few blocks from the ferry that links the islands to Canada’s Newfoundland, 16 miles away. “Too much so.”

Tourists boarding the ferry to the islands — so close to Canada but a far-flung territory of France — are now warned to secure lodging first.

“Everything is booked solid,” Mr. Abraham said, adding that many visitors were unable to find places to stay or even eat.

Capping a year of unusual attention, the territory will be the setting this weekend for a meeting between President Emmanuel Macron of France and Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada with the aim of “reasserting national sovereignty” in the face of American expansionism. The visit on Sunday by Mr. Carney — whose push to make Canada less dependent on the United States rests greatly on his ambitions to forge closer ties with Europe — will be the first by a Canadian leader to the islands.

The archipelago of three islands and a few islets is sheltered from the open Atlantic by the far larger Newfoundland. A small fraction of the territory’s 6,000 French citizens live on the biggest island, Miquelon, with most in Saint Pierre, the site of the local government and the representative of the French government.
